verses.1: Al-Mizan supplies the unfinished conditional’s complement from (84:6): when these events occur, people meet their Lord for reckoning and recompense. Inshiqāq is the sky’s cracking open, one sign of the Hour alongside the earth’s spreading (84:3), the sun’s winding up (81:1), falling stars (82:2), and the sun and moon’s joining (75:9). Idhn, giving ear, is figurative submission and obedience; ḥuqqat means that humble obedience to its Lord is fitting for the sky. An editor notes that using the past tense for this future event signifies its certainty.

verses.3: Al-Mizan reads the earth’s spreading as its stretching and transformation (14:48), and its emptying as casting out every dead person within it. It reports alternatives that it expels both the dead and treasures, or sheds its mountains and seas, but finds its own reading clearer. As with the sky in 84:2, the earth gives ear to its Lord in obedient submission.

verses.6: Al-Mizan gives kadḥ two compatible senses: striving and toil, or labor whose effects impress the soul; because it is directed ilā the Lord, each implies a journey. Every human being, as a servant owned and directed by the Lord, inevitably travels toward Him and may neither will nor act apart from what He wills and commands, for actions are accountable. Encountering God is thus the state in which His rule and judgment alone operate and no intermediate cause veils servants from Him. The generic al-insān shows that this Lordship applies to all humanity. The verse consequently argues for resurrection: Lordship entails servitude, servitude accountability, accountability return for reckoning, reckoning payment, and payment resurrection. An editor notes that the preceding future scene’s past tense marks certainty.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes the record in the right hand as the record of deeds, following the return to God implied by (84:6); an editor refers to earlier discussions in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ and Sūrah al-Ḥāqqah. Easy reckoning means leniency without exacting scrutiny. In this context ahl, family or folk, most plausibly means the heavenly beings assigned to the person, including houris and ghilmān, to whom he returns joyfully. The alternatives—his believing earthly family already in paradise, or believers generally as brethren—are not quite apparent.

verses.10: Al-Mizan suggests, tentatively, that records are given from behind because the recipients’ faces have been turned backward (4:47). This does not conflict with receiving a book in the left hand (69:25), and the commentary reserves the fuller meaning of receiving it from behind for its narrations. An authorial note explains that an omitted min, ‘from,’ accounts for warāʾ being accusative through nazʿ al-khāfiḍ. Thubūr is like wayl, destruction or loss, and praying for it is the cry wā thubūrāh; the recipient then enters an indescribably blazing fire and suffers its immense heat.

verses.13: Al-Mizan says the condemned person’s joy among family was attachment to worldly possessions and ornament, which made him forget the hereafter; such wrongful exultation is condemned in (40:75). His supposition that he would not yaḥūr means denying return to his Lord for reckoning and retribution. Absorption in sin and wrongdoing diverts attention from the hereafter and makes resurrection seem a remote myth. An editor glosses the preceding cry of thubūr as despair and regret, with parallels at (19:23), (25:13-14), (43:77), (69:27), and (78:40); an authorial note says yaḥūru is synonymous with yarjiʿu, ‘return.’

verses.15: Al-Mizan takes balā as rejecting the supposition that there is no return: the person will return because his Lord, his Owner and Director, sees all he does, has imposed obligations, and has set recompense for deeds. This is an argument for the afterlife. It infers that the distribution of records and unrolling of scrolls precede reckoning, supported by (17:13-14). Narrations through Sunni and Shiʿa chains say believers guilty of major sins enter hell temporarily and leave through the Prophet’s intercession, yet these verses identify those receiving records from behind as disbelievers and those receiving them in the right hand as people promised easy reckoning and paradise. Al-Mizan rejects the suggestion that sinful believers receive their records after leaving hell because that reverses the sequence; it also rejects giving them the left hand because the relevant left-hand verses likewise concern disbelievers, and rejects giving them the right hand while excluding them from easy reckoning because the verses deliberately distinguish the felicitous from the wretched and contain a promise unsuited to them. It allows that their reckoning could be easy only relative to eternally damned disbelievers, though hard beside the Godwary. More fundamentally, the two groups may be non-exhaustive extremes: (56:7-11) distinguishes the Foremost, and (9:106) leaves al-mustaḍʿafūn awaiting God’s verdict. Thus right-hand recipients are the Godwary in paradise and left-hand recipients those eternally in hell; the verses present exemplary paths of taqwā and disobedience, not every case. An editor summarizes two remaining possibilities for sinful believers: they receive the right hand but a more meticulous reckoning, or their status is beyond this passage’s scope.
verses.16: Al-Mizan defines shafaq as the red, yellow, and white hues on the horizon at sunset and nightfall. An editor summarizes two possible conclusions concerning sinful believers: they may receive their records in the right hand but undergo more meticulous reckoning than the Godwary, or their situation cannot be known from these verses.
verses.17: Al-Mizan defines wasaqa as gathering and bringing together: creatures disperse by day and retire home at night. It reports an alternative reading, ṭarada, in which the night drives stars from concealment into view.
verses.18: Al-Mizan defines ittisāq as gathering and completing: the oath is by the moon as its light comes together until it is full.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes (84:19) as the complement to the preceding oaths and as addressed to all people. Ṭabaq can mean correspondence or matching, but here denotes the connected stages of humanity’s arduous journey to its Lord: worldly life, death, barzakh, passage to the hereafter, life there, reckoning, and recompense. The oaths emphasize (84:6) and resurrection, prepare the rebuke of unbelief in (84:20), and frame the later warning and glad tidings in (84:24-25).
verses.20: Al-Mizan reads (84:20-21) as rhetorical questions of surprise and rebuke. The third-person address signals that God turns from a people who ignore His reminder and exhortation to address the Prophet about their refusal to believe and prostrate when the Qur’an is recited.

verses.22: Al-Mizan says the present tense of yukadhdhibūna marks persistent denial, and calling them faithless identifies the cause of that denial. Īʿāʾ, to harbor, is putting something in a container: they do not reject faith because its message lacks proof, but through attachment to forefathers and chiefs, becoming rooted in disbelief and continuing denial. God knows the disbelief and polytheism accumulated and hidden in their hearts. The alternative that they harbor unrelated, ineffable secrets is not congruous with the context.

verses.24: Al-Mizan takes the initial fāʾ as drawing painful punishment from the faithless’ preceding denial. Tabshīr, normally giving glad tidings, is applied to punishment with irony and mockery. The faithful who do righteous deeds are an unconnected exception to ‘them’; their ghayr mamnūn reward is unfailing and free of any burdening, humiliation, or abuse.
